69. The Miracle of Fàtima

🍀For Colin🍀

The Miracle of Fátima is the most widely recognised miracle in modern Catholicism, reportedly witnessed by almost 100,000 individuals. On October 13, 1917, a vast crowd assembled in the town of Fátima, Portugal, in response to claims made by three shepherd children, Lúcia, Francisco and Jacinta, that the Virgin Mary had appeared to them and foretold her return on that date to perform a public miracle. The event garnered substantial public and media attention, attracting devout believers but also skeptics, journalists and photographers seeking to observe and document the event.

During WW I, Portugal was gripped by hardship and despair, with widespread sentiments of war and revolution. When the shepherd children in the mountainous village of Fátima claimed to have been visited by angels, their accounts offered renewed hope to a disillusioned nation. Following the assassination of the King of Portugal and the subsequent abolition of the monarchy, the new government, dominated by Freemasons who valued science and progress over religion, implemented strict anti-clerical policies. Religious activities were suppressed, devotees arrested or exiled and the anti-Catholic laws enacted in 1911 rendered 'visions' both subversive and intolerable.

At this time, approximately 70 per cent of the peasant population in Portugal was illiterate and education was limited to agricultural labour skills. They were a simple yet devout people. Observers noted that the messages reported in the Fátima apparitions were theologically sophisticated, far beyond what uneducated children could be expected to articulate. Out of fear and skepticism, even their families doubted their claims, yet despite ridicule and hostility, the children remained steadfast in their conviction and consistent in their accounts.

During the reported miracle, numerous witnesses claimed that the silver sun appeared to dance, spin, or zigzag across the sky, plunge toward the Earth and emit radiant, multicoloured light. These phenomena allegedly lasted for about ten minutes. However, prolonged direct observation of the sun can cause solar retinopathy, leading to visual distortions such as bright colours and the illusion of movement, effects consistent with many descriptions from that day.

Some scholars have suggested the possibility of deliberate tampering with the water supply of the town, potentially inducing hallucinatory experiences among those gathered; however, not all witnesses reported observing any unusual phenomena. Photographers present at the scene captured no evidence of extraordinary occurrences, focusing instead on documenting the crowds of kneeling worshippers holding rosary beads. Given that photographic technology was already well developed and widely accessible, the absence of visual confirmation remains notable.

Is it also conceivable that the power of suggestion, intensified by the social and emotional strain of wartime, contributed to collective perception or belief? The children claimed to have witnessed visions of hell and demonic suffering so terrifying that they were overcome with fear until the Virgin Mary revealed a vision of heaven. As the sun 'rushed' toward the Earth, many in the crowd reportedly experienced similar terror. Concerned about potential government reprisal, the townspeople refrained from sharing accounts of the event until after the 1917 apparitions became widely known. Fear is the ultimate controller in the chaos of war.

Is it possible that the angelic apparitions of the late 1800s and early 1900s were manufactured by some kind of technology unknown to the people, such as the purported Project Blue Beam or a CGI effect? What kind of power would this have over Catholic countries during what was known as the Great War? Moreover, how would it affect peasant people without education? Could this event have truly been a miracle or perhaps even some kind of satanic deception? Notably, few of the prophecies eventuated. Both Fransisco and Jacinta died in a flu pandemic shortly after the apparitions.
